summary: Defines a YANG data model and mechanisms that let a subscriber ask a publisher for a customized, continuous stream of events. A subscriber can set up subscriptions so it receives only the information it wants, as generated by the publisher.

plainLanguage.summary: A device that keeps a log of what has happened can now let a monitoring system ask for exactly the parts it cares about, and keep sending them as they happen. The rules for asking, and the rules for what may be sent to whom, are set out here in a form that does not depend on how the two talk to each other.

questions: how to subscribe to yang events
what is a yang event stream
subtitle: A transport-independent way to subscribe to a device's event streams and get a customised, continuous feed.

tldr.problem: Earlier NETCONF notification subscriptions were tied to NETCONF and limited: one subscription per session, no changes in flight, no per-subscription counters.
tldr.mechanism: A YANG data model and RPCs let a subscriber establish, modify, delete or kill dynamic subscriptions to named event streams, with filters, QoS, replay and stop times. Configured subscriptions can instead be installed through configuration, and the publisher reports changes with subscription state change notifications.
tldr.outcome: A publisher can push filtered event records to receivers over any transport that meets the stated requirements, with bindings for NETCONF and RESTCONF defined elsewhere.

today: RFC 8639 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2019. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The bindings that carry these notifications over NETCONF and RESTCONF are defined in other documents.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The document defines a YANG data model and associated mechanisms enabling subscriber-specific subscriptions to a publisher's event streams. This effectively enables a 'subscribe, then publish' capability where the customized information needs and access permissions of each target receiver are understood by the publisher before subscribed event records are marshaled and pushed. The receiver then gets a continuous, customized feed of publisher-generated information.

While the functionality defined in the document is transport agnostic, transports like NETCONF or RESTCONF can be used to configure or dynamically signal subscriptions. Bindings for subscribed event record delivery for NETCONF and RESTCONF are defined in other documents. The YANG data model defined here conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture.

The primary motivation was to resolve the limitations of the earlier subscription model, which were alleviated to some extent by an earlier requirements document. The key capabilities supported here include multiple subscriptions on a single transport session; support for dynamic and configured subscriptions; modification of an existing subscription in progress; per-subscription operational counters; negotiation of subscription parameters, through the use of hints returned as part of declined subscription requests; subscription state change notifications such as publisher-driven suspension and parameter modification; and independence from transport.
sections.plainLanguage: A subscriber can now ask for the specific events it cares about, change its mind while the feed is running, and work over more than one transport. The publisher applies each subscriber's own permissions before it sends anything.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
The document uses the terms client, configuration, configuration datastore, subscriber and publisher as defined by the Network Management Datastore Architecture, and defines the rest itself.

A configured subscription is a subscription installed via configuration into a configuration datastore. A dynamic subscription is a subscription created dynamically by a subscriber via a Remote Procedure Call. An event is an occurrence of something that may be of interest, such as a configuration change, a fault, a change in status, crossing a threshold, or an external input to the system. The event occurrence time is a timestamp matching the time an originating process identified as when an event happened. An event record is a set of information detailing an event, and an event stream is a continuous, chronologically ordered set of events aggregated under some context.

An event stream filter is evaluation criteria that may be applied against event records in an event stream, and event records pass the filter when the specified criteria are met. A notification message is information intended for a receiver indicating that one or more events have occurred. A publisher is an entity responsible for streaming notification messages per the terms of a subscription. A receiver is a target to which a publisher pushes subscribed event records, and for dynamic subscriptions the receiver and the subscriber are the same entity. A subscriber is a client able to request and negotiate a contract for the generation and push of event records from a publisher, and again for dynamic subscriptions the receiver and subscriber are the same entity. A subscription is a contract with a publisher, stipulating the information that one or more receivers wish to have pushed from the publisher without the need for further solicitation.
sections.plainLanguage: An event is something that happened. An event record is the description of it. An event stream is an ordered run of such records. A subscription is the deal between the publisher and the subscriber about which records the subscriber gets.

sections.title: Dynamic and Configured Subscriptions
sections.content:
The document describes a transport-agnostic mechanism for subscribing to and receiving content from an event stream in a publisher, operating through the use of a subscription. Two types of subscriptions are supported.

Dynamic subscriptions are ones where a subscriber initiates a subscription negotiation with a publisher via an RPC. If the publisher is able to serve the request, it accepts it and then starts pushing notification messages back to the subscriber. If the publisher cannot serve it as requested, an error response is returned, and that response MAY include hints for subscription parameters which, had they been present, might have enabled the request to be accepted.

Configured subscriptions allow the management of subscriptions via configuration, so that a publisher can send notification messages to a receiver. Support for configured subscriptions is optional, with its availability advertised via a YANG feature.

The lifetime of a dynamic subscription is bound by the transport session used to establish it. For connection-oriented stateful transports like NETCONF, the loss of the transport session results in the immediate termination of any associated dynamic subscriptions. For connectionless or stateless transports like HTTP, a lack of receipt acknowledgment of a sequential set of notification messages, or of keep-alives, can trigger a termination. A configured subscription instead lives for as long as the relevant configuration is present in the publisher's applied configuration. Being tied to configuration operations implies that configured subscriptions can be configured to persist across reboots, and that a configured subscription can persist even when its publisher is fully disconnected from any network.

Configured subscriptions can be modified by any configuration client with write permission on the configuration of the subscription. Dynamic subscriptions can only be modified via an RPC request made by the original subscriber, or by a change to configuration data referenced by the subscription. There is no mixing of dynamic and configured operations on a single subscription: a configured subscription cannot be modified or deleted using the RPCs defined in the document, and a dynamic subscription cannot be directly modified or deleted by configuration operations. It is, however, possible to perform a configuration operation that indirectly impacts a dynamic subscription, since changing the value of a preconfigured filter referenced by an existing dynamic subscription may change the event records passed to a receiver.

A publisher MAY terminate a dynamic subscription at any time, and MAY decide to temporarily suspend the sending of notification messages for any dynamic subscription, or for one or more receivers of a configured subscription. Such termination or suspension is driven by internal considerations of the publisher.
sections.plainLanguage: A dynamic subscription lives only as long as the connection that created it. A configured subscription is written into the publisher's configuration, so it survives a restart and can be kept when the network is down.

sections.title: Event Streams and Filters
sections.content:
An event stream is a named entity on a publisher, exposing a continuously updating set of YANG-defined event records. An event record is an instantiation of a 'notification' YANG statement, and if the notification is defined as a child to a data node, the instantiation includes the hierarchy of nodes that identifies the data node in the datastore. Each event stream is available for subscription. How event streams are defined, how event records are defined and generated, and how event records are assigned to streams are out of scope.

There is only one reserved event stream name in the document: 'NETCONF'. That event stream contains all NETCONF event record information supported by the publisher, except where an event record has explicitly been excluded. Beyond it, implementations MAY define additional event streams. The publisher maintains a list of available event streams as operational data, containing both standardized and vendor-specific event streams, so that subscribers can discover what streams a publisher supports. That list also reports whether a stream supports replay and when its replay log was created and aged.

As YANG-defined event records are created by a system, they may be assigned to one or more streams. An event record is distributed to a subscription's receivers where the subscription includes the identified stream and subscription filtering does not exclude the record. Access control permissions may be used to silently exclude event records from an event stream for which the receiver has no read access. If no access control permissions are in place for event records on an event stream, a receiver MUST be allowed access to all the event records. If subscriber permissions change during the lifecycle of a subscription and event stream access is no longer permitted, the subscription MUST be terminated. Event records MUST NOT be delivered to a receiver in a different order than the order in which they were placed on an event stream.

The filtering mechanism is extensible. The filter is a boolean test placed on the content of an event record, and a 'false' filtering result causes the event record to be excluded from delivery to a receiver. A filter never results in information being stripped from an event record. The two optional filtering syntaxes supported are XPath and subtree. If no event stream filter is provided in a subscription, all event records on the stream are to be sent. The 'filters' container maintains a list of all subscription filters that persist outside the lifecycle of a single subscription, so that predefined filters may be referenced by more than one subscription.
sections.plainLanguage: A publisher offers named streams of events. The subscriber names a stream and can add a test that decides which records from it are worth sending. Records the subscriber is not allowed to see are quietly left out.

sections.title: Quality of Service Parameters
sections.content:
Several Quality of Service parameters indicate the treatment of a subscription relative to other traffic between publisher and receiver. A 'dscp' marking differentiates the prioritisation of notification messages during network transit. A 'weighting' allows bandwidth proportional to that weighting to be allocated to a subscription relative to other subscriptions. A 'dependency' expresses a dependency upon another subscription.

If the publisher supports the 'dscp' feature, a subscription with a 'dscp' leaf MUST result in a corresponding Differentiated Services Code Point marking being placed in the IP header of any resulting notification messages and subscription state change notifications, and the publisher MUST respect those markings for subscription traffic egressing that publisher. Different DSCP code points require different transport connections, so where TCP is used a publisher that supports the 'dscp' feature must ensure that a subscription's notification messages are returned in a single TCP transport session where all traffic shares the subscription's 'dscp' leaf value. If this cannot be guaranteed, an 'establish-subscription' RPC request SHOULD be rejected with a 'dscp-unavailable' error.

For the 'weighting' parameter, when concurrently dequeuing notification messages from multiple subscriptions to a receiver, the publisher MUST allocate bandwidth to each subscription in proportion to the weights assigned to those subscriptions. Weighting is an optional capability, identified via the 'qos' feature. If a subscription has the 'dependency' parameter set, any buffered notification messages containing event records selected by the parent subscription MUST be dequeued prior to the notification messages of the dependent subscription, and if notification messages have dependencies on each other, the one queued the longest goes first. A dependency that references a subscription which does not exist, or is no longer accessible to that subscriber, MUST be silently removed. The dependency and weighting parameters will only be respected and enforced between subscriptions that share the same 'dscp' leaf value.
sections.plainLanguage: A subscriber can ask for its feed to be marked with a priority, to get a share of bandwidth proportional to a weight, and to be sent after another subscription's messages.

sections.title: Dynamic Subscriptions
sections.content:
Dynamic subscriptions are managed via protocol operations, in the form of RPCs, made against targets located in the publisher. These RPCs are designed extensibly so that they may be augmented for subscription targets beyond event streams.

The publisher's state machine for a dynamic subscription matters: such a subscription does not exist at the publisher until an 'establish-subscription' RPC is accepted, and the mere request by a subscriber is not enough for it to become externally visible. Successful 'establish-subscription' or 'modify-subscription' RPCs move the subscription to the active state, while a failed 'modify-subscription' RPC leaves the subscription in its previous state with no visible change to any streaming updates. A 'delete-subscription' or 'kill-subscription' RPC ends the subscription, as does reaching a 'stop-time'. A publisher may choose to suspend a subscription when there is not sufficient CPU or bandwidth available to service it, and this is announced with the 'subscription-suspended' state change notification. A suspended subscription may be modified by the subscriber, for example in an attempt to use fewer resources, and a successful modification returns it to the active state. Even without a modification request, a publisher may return a subscription to the active state when sufficient resources are again available, announced with the 'subscription-resumed' notification.

The 'establish-subscription' RPC allows a subscriber to request the creation of a subscription. Its input parameters are a 'stream' name identifying the targeted event stream; an event stream filter, which may reduce the set of event records pushed; an optional 'encoding' for the event records pushed if the transport supports multiple encodings, with the encoding of the RPC used if none is given; an optional 'stop-time', after which notification messages stop; and an optional 'replay-start-time', which MUST be in the past and indicates that the subscriber is requesting a replay of previously generated information, with the subscription starting immediately if there is none. If the publisher can satisfy the request it replies with an identifier for the subscription and immediately starts streaming notification messages.

The error responses carry three transport-independent error structures that let the publisher supply information that does not fit into the existing transport-layer RPC structures: 'establish-subscription-stream-error-info', which MUST be returned if an RPC error reason has not been placed elsewhere in the transport portion of a failed response and MUST be sent if hints on how to overcome the error are included; 'modify-subscription-stream-error-info', with the same rule for a failed modification; and 'delete-subscription-error-info', which MUST be returned with the reason populated for a failed deletion or kill.
sections.plainLanguage: A subscription starts when the publisher accepts the request, and it can be changed, suspended, resumed or ended while it runs. If the publisher cannot do what was asked, it says why and hints at what would have worked.

sections.title: Event Record Delivery and State Changes
sections.content:
Whether dynamic or configured, once a subscription has been set up, the publisher streams event records via notification messages per the terms of the subscription. For dynamic subscriptions the messages are sent over the session used to establish the subscription; for configured subscriptions they are sent over the connections specified by the transport and each receiver.

A notification message is sent to a receiver when an event record is not blocked by either the specified filter criteria or receiver permissions. It MUST include an eventTime object, and that object MUST be at the top level of a YANG structured event record. When a dynamic subscription has been started or modified, event records matching the newly applied filter criteria MUST NOT be sent until after the RPC reply has been sent; when a configured subscription has been started or modified, they MUST NOT be sent until after the corresponding notification has been sent.

In addition to sending event records, a publisher MUST also send subscription state change notifications when events related to subscription management have occurred. These are unlike other notifications in that they are never included in any event stream. Instead they are inserted into the sequence of notification messages sent to a particular receiver. They cannot be dropped or filtered out, they cannot be stored in replay buffers, and they are delivered only to the impacted receivers of a subscription. The identification of subscription state change notifications is easy to separate from other notification messages through the use of the YANG extension 'subscription-state-notif', which tags a notification as such.

The complete set is 'subscription-started', which indicates that a configured subscription has started and event records may be sent and carries all the parameters of the subscription except transport connection information and origin information; 'subscription-modified'; 'subscription-terminated'; 'subscription-suspended'; 'subscription-resumed'; 'subscription-completed'; and 'replay-completed'. For dynamic subscriptions, no 'subscription-started' notification is ever sent.
sections.plainLanguage: The publisher pushes records to the subscriber as they happen. Separately, it tells the subscriber about changes to the subscription itself, such as it being suspended or ended, and those messages are never filtered out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The YANG module specified in the document defines a schema for data designed to be accessed via network management protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF. The lowest NETCONF layer is the secure transport layer, and the mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH. The lowest RESTCONF layer is HTTPS, and the mandatory-to-implement secure transport is TLS. The Network Configuration Access Control Model provides the means to restrict access for particular NETCONF or RESTCONF users to a preconfigured subset of all available operations and content.

With configured subscriptions, one or more publishers could be used to overwhelm a receiver. To counter this, notification messages SHOULD NOT be sent to any receiver that does not support this specification, and receivers that do not want notification messages need only terminate or refuse any transport sessions from the publisher. When a receiver of a configured subscription gets a new 'subscription-started' message for a known subscription where it is already consuming events, it may indicate that an attacker has done something that has momentarily disrupted receiver connectivity. To acquire events lost during the interval, the receiver SHOULD retrieve any event records generated since the last event record was received, which can be done by establishing a separate dynamic replay subscription with the same filtering criteria, assuming the publisher supports the 'replay' feature.

For dynamic subscriptions, implementations need to protect against malicious or buggy subscribers that may send a large number of 'establish-subscription' requests and so use up system resources. Operators SHOULD monitor for such cases and, if discovered, take remedial action to limit the resources used, such as suspending or terminating a subset of the subscriptions or terminating the underlying transport session.

The replay mechanisms provide access to historical event records. By design, the access control model that protects these records could enable subscribers to view data to which they were not authorized at the time of collection. Using DNS names for a configured subscription's receiver lookups can cause situations where the name resolves differently than expected on the publisher, so the recipient would be different than expected. An attacker that can cause the publisher to use an incorrect time can induce message replay by setting the time in the past, and can introduce a risk of message loss by setting the time in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: A subscriber that opens many subscriptions at once could tie up the publisher, so operators should watch for that. And a subscriber may be able to see old records it would not be allowed to see today, because the rules that applied when they were recorded may have been looser.
